questions.q_en:
The sentence below contains errors. Select the option with the correct use of tenses.

Your father will waiting for you when you reach home.
options_en: Your father should waiting for you when you reach home.
Your father will be waiting for you when you reach home.
Your father would waiting for you when you reach home.
Your father waiting for you when you reach home.
questions.solution_en:
The original sentence uses will waiting, which is incorrect because "will" requires the base verb form, and the correct structure for future continuous is "will be + verb-ing." The sentence describes a future action (father waiting when you arrive).

A: "should waiting" is incorrect; "should" pairs with the base verb (e.g., "should wait").

B: "will be waiting" correctly uses future continuous for an ongoing action at a future point.

C: "would waiting" is incorrect; "would" pairs with the base verb (e.g., "would wait").

D: "waiting" lacks an auxiliary, making it incomplete for future tense.

Thus, Your father will be waiting for you when you reach home is correct.

questions.q_en:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution'.

Having been declared the winner of the prestigious literary award, the author's novel quickly became a national bestseller, attracting praise from critics and readers across the country.
options_en: the novel of the author quickly became
the author saw his novel quickly become
the author's novel had quickly become
questions.solution_en:
The original sentence contains a dangling modifier. The introductory participle phrase "Having been declared the winner..." must modify the subject of the main clause. The current subject is "the author's novel," which illogically suggests that the novel itself was declared the winner, not the author. The subject must be the author.

Option b) the author saw his novel quickly become corrects the error by making "the author" the subject of the main clause. The author was declared the winner, so the modifier is now logically connected.

Option a) the novel of the author quickly became does not fix the dangling modifier, as the subject is still "the novel."

Option c) the author's novel had quickly become also fails to correct the error and uses an unnecessary past perfect tense.

So, the correct sentence is: Having been declared the winner of the prestigious literary award, the author saw his novel quickly become a national bestseller, attracting praise from critics and readers across the country.

Hence, the most appropriate choice is b) the author saw his novel quickly become.

questions.q_en:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice:

"Someone has taken my secret diary."
options_en: My secret diary had been taken by someone.
My secret diary has to be taken by someone.
My secret diary has been taken by someone.
My secret diary will have been taken by someone.
questions.solution_en:
The subject of the Active Voice is changed into the object of the Passive voice. Also, the object of the Active Voice is changed into the subject of the Passive Voice.

The usage of a "to be" form of verb is necessary while changing the voice of the sentence from Active to Passive.

In Passive Voice, the preposition "by" is used before the object. However, it is optional in some cases.

The Active voice in this question is in Present Perfect. Thus, the Passive voice will also be in Present Perfect.

The format of Active voice is: Subject + has/have + V3 + Object.

Thus, in Passive voice, the format will be: Object of the active voice (Subjective case) + has/have + been + V3 + by + Subject of the active voice (Objective case).

For example:

Arya has bought a new horse. (Active Voice)

A new horse has been bought by Arya. (Passive Voice)

The options except (3) don't follow the correct grammatical format of the Passive Voice.

questions.q_en:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in the positive degree of comparison.

She is the most generous person I know.
options_en: She is more generous among the people I know.
A generous person among the people I know she is.
No other person I know is as generous as she is.
Among the people I know of all is she generous.
questions.solution_en:
The given sentence is in the superlative degree, which means it compares one thing or person with all the others in a group and shows that it has the highest degree of quality. The superlative degree is formed by using the word most before the adjective. To change a sentence from the superlative degree to the positive degree, we need to remove the word 'most' before the adjective and use 'no other' or 'none' before it.

Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.

Option (a) is in comparative degree.

Options (b) and (d) are grammatically incoherent.

Note:

Adjectives: Words which are used with a noun/pronoun to describe or point out, the person, animal, place, or thing which the noun names, or to tell the number or quantity, are called Adjectives.

· The Positive Degree is used to denote the mere existence of some quality of what we speak about. It is used when no comparison is made.

· The Comparative degree denotes a higher degree of quality than the positive and is used when two things are compared.

· The Superlative degree indicates the highest degree of quality and is used when more than two things (or sets of things) are compared.

Little that I knew of the English language was not sufficient to make me an English teacher.

The sentence is: "Little that I knew of the English language was not sufficient to make me an English teacher."

· The original phrase "Little that I knew" is awkward. In English, "little" as a quantifier can be used in different forms: "a little" (a small amount, positive), "the little" (the small amount that exists), or "little" (not much, negative). The intended meaning here is "the small amount of knowledge I had," which should be followed by a positive statement, but the sentence uses a double negative ("was not sufficient"), making it confusing.

· Option 1: "So little" - This would make the sentence "So little that I knew of the English language was not sufficient," which is still awkward due to the double negative. It doesn't improve clarity.

· Option 2: "A little" - This means a small amount (positive), so "A little that I knew of the English language was not sufficient" implies some knowledge, but the double negative makes it confusing.

· Option 3: "The little" - This fits best. "The little" refers to the small amount of knowledge the speaker had. The corrected sentence becomes: "The little that I knew of the English language was not sufficient to make me an English teacher," meaning the small amount of knowledge I had wasn't enough. This resolves the awkwardness while maintaining the intended meaning.

· Option 4: "Very little" - This would make the sentence "Very little that I knew of the English language was not sufficient," which is grammatically awkward and doesn't improve the sentence.

Option 3 ("The little") is the most appropriate substitution.

"Oh, Mary, please don't be moody, not today. I told Harry all about how polite and intelligent and cheerful you are," she said. Harry was my mother's new boyfriend, her "significant other," she called him. She'd met him at a business meeting when her company bought the company Harry worked for, and since then she'd been driving over the border to Canada every weekend to see him, leaving me at Dad's. Don't get me wrong, I loved staying with Dad, but I missed my Mom-weekends. We used to make popcorn and watch late-night TV, then sleep in and eat cold breakfast cereal together. Now, when she came to pick me up on Sunday afternoons, she always looked glowing and energetic - and much happier than she ever looked after a weekend spent with me. Last Monday she said something about her and Harry getting married, and that this trip might be the time when he pops the question. The only obstacle before him was meeting me. "I'll be sugar and spice and everything nice, I promise," I said sarcastically, staring out at the Canadian countryside. It pretty much resembled the American countryside only . . . it was more Canadian, somehow. Bigger and emptier, just as I imagined Harry; bigger than Dad, with an enormous head with lots of empty space inside.

Finally, sentence C provides a concluding statement on the broader scientific importance of "These unique ecosystems," linking them to the search for extraterrestrial life.

Hence, option (c) is the answer.

questions.q_en:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.

The island is / surround by/ sharks and / rare marine creatures.
questions.solution_en:
In the part mentioned in option (d), the verb 'surround' which is in the base form (V1) incorrectly follows the verb 'is' which requires the verb that follows it to be in either Past participle form (V3) or continuous/present participle form (V4). Accordingly, the past participle form of the verb 'surrounded' is to be used instead of 'surround' since the sentence is in the passive voice. The subject 'island' is what the action 'surrounded' is subjected to.

The correct sentence is: The island is surrounded by sharks and rare marine creatures.

Hence, the correct answer is option (d).

Note:

V1 -> Base form/simple form of verb, V2 -> Past form of verb (-ed form or irregular verb), V3 -> Past participle form of verb (-ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n), V4 -> Continuous form of verb / Present participle form of verb (-ing form), V5 -> Third person singular (V1+ -es or -s).

Active and Passive Voice: When the person doing the action is the subject, the sentence is said to be in active form/voice. When the subject is what the action is directed at, then the sentence is said to be in passive form/voice. For example: Active Voice: Rita and her friends performed a skit. Here 'Rita and her friends' (subject) perform the action. Passive Voice: A skit was performed by Rita and her friends. Here 'skit' is the subject (at which the action is directed).

questions.q_en:
Directions : Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow.

Environmental or genetic influences antisocial conduct of a human being, which has an impact on behaviour, such as conduct disorder. In a recent study conducted, young people with conduct disorders had their brains examined, along with controls that were healthy and did not have the disease. The thickness of various regions of the cortex and the brain's outer layer was measured using the scanned images. It was demonstrated in the study that conduct disorder is a psychiatric condition rather than adolescent disobedience. Awareness, perception, attention, memory and language are all impacted by the cortex. The findings of the study were unexpected. They demonstrated distinct disparities between adolescents whose behavioural issues began in adolescence and those whose issues began earlier in life. Although both groups were different from healthy controls, it was discovered that distinct regions of the cortex in the teenagers who had experienced early-onset behavioural issues were thicker in comparison to the healthy participants.

Which of the following is NOT impacted by the cortex?
questions.solution_en:
As per the following excerpt from the passage, "It was demonstrated in the study that conduct disorder is a psychiatric condition rather than adolescent disobedience. Awareness, perception, attention, memory and language are all impacted by the cortex," it can be noted that the cortex impacts awareness, perception, attention, memory, and language, but disobedience is a behaviour, not a cognitive function directly impacted by the cortex.

Memory and attention: Both are impacted by the cortex.

Language and awareness: Both are impacted by the cortex.

Memory and perception: Both are impacted by the cortex.

Hence, the correct answer is option (a).

questions.q_en:
Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

She will being studying for her exams tomorrow.
questions.solution_en: The sentence "She will being studying for her exams tomorrow" has a grammatical error in the underlined part "will being." In English, the future continuous tense is formed using "will be" followed by the present participle of the verb (e.g., "studying"). The phrase "will being" is incorrect because "being" is not the appropriate verb form here; it should be "will be studying." The correct sentence is "She will be studying for her exams tomorrow." The other underlined parts - "studying," "exams," and "tomorrow" - are correct in context. Therefore, the error is in option 3.
